title: DOJ opens antitrust review of NVIDIA's $20B Groq licensing deal
subtitle: Regulators are examining whether the December licensing structure — non-exclusive, cash-heavy, and without an equity purchase — was designed to avoid Hart-Scott-Rodino review.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: The US Department of Justice has opened an antitrust review of the $20 billion licensing agreement NVIDIA reached with Groq in December 2025, according to reporting from Bloomberg and the New York Times on September 10, 2026. DOJ has sent NVIDIA a formal request for information covering the structure of the deal — a non-exclusive license to Groq's LPU technology that transferred rights and cash without an equity purchase. That structure appears to have kept the transaction below the reporting thresholds under the Hart-Scott-Rodino Act, and DOJ is examining whether that was the point.

The question at issue is not whether NVIDIA and Groq are competitors — they are, in inference. The question is whether a $20B licensing deal between the market's dominant training-chip supplier and one of its most-watched inference-chip challengers is functionally a merger that was papered as something else. If DOJ concludes yes, the enforcement toolkit ranges from fines to a consent decree that restricts how NVIDIA uses the licensed IP. Bloomberg's report noted that forcing NVIDIA to unwind the deal is considered unlikely; the more probable outcome is a settlement that constrains how NVIDIA can bundle Groq-derived features into its own stack.

The macro read is that antitrust posture toward AI hardware is hardening. The Nvidia-MediaTek NVLink Fusion deal on September 2 was paused for antitrust review; the Nvidia-AI-compute partnership on August 29 was paused for the same reason; and this Groq inquiry now names NVIDIA's biggest single-deal transaction. Regulators appear to have decided that vertical integration in AI chips is where the concentration risk lives, and the licensing-not-acquiring pattern that hyperscalers and chipmakers have adopted through 2026 is going to get read as attempted evasion by default. That will change how these deals get structured for the rest of the decade.

Takeaway for learners: if you are considering a career in AI hardware or policy, the current period is the analog of the 1998 Microsoft antitrust case — the legal framework for the AI industry's competitive structure is being written right now. Read the DOJ complaints as they come out; they will tell you what regulators think a competitive AI market looks like, and where the industry is going to have to build differently. The lawyers and economists arguing these cases will shape a decade of investment.
